overview: Benevento was a Lombard duchy and later a principality, but this imported record runs from 1000 to 1279, across the end of its ruling dynasty in 1077 and into papal government. Its later outline wrongly includes Sicily and greatly exaggerates Benevento’s territory. This card follows the city’s final Lombard rulers and its medieval life afterward; it does not describe a Beneventan state ruling that entire polygon.

periods.title: A papal city
periods.summary: Benevento continued under papal government, interrupted by regional conflicts.

sections.title: A changing government, a continuing city

items.text: Benevento’s inhabitants accepted papal authority in 1051 after expelling their princes. The rulers returned in 1055, but their authority was increasingly subordinate to the pope. This uneven transition explains why 1077, the death of the last Lombard prince Landulf VI, is a dynastic endpoint rather than the first moment anyone considered papal government.

Under the popes, Benevento developed local institutions as well as papal administration. The oldest surviving version of its city statutes dates to 1202. Consuls exercised local jurisdiction, although their powers changed and were contested. Medieval government could involve argument among citizens, officeholders and distant rulers, rather than one person making every decision.

Some houses connected across streets by raised passages called pontili. Permission from the ruler was required, and the street underneath had to remain public. A family might gain a convenient route between properties while everybody else still needed room to pass below.

A will dated December 1092 records a house with a fireplace. Other homes had upper floors reached by outside masonry stairs. These details distinguish particular buildings from a fantasy of identical medieval cottages. Comfort and construction varied from household to household.

Benevento’s documented crafts included pottery, shoemaking, tailoring, carpentry, stoneworking and metalwork. Mills operated along the rivers, especially a channel diverted from the Sabato. These activities connected the city to farms and waterpower: a prince’s court needed a much larger working community around it.

At Sant’Ilario a Port’Aurea, archaeologists studied a rubbish deposit in a chamber probably first used as an ossuary. Its pottery dates from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, after Lombard rule and partly after this map interval. Bowls, jugs, cooking pots and large storage vessels preserve the equipment of meals and provisions.

Laboratory analysis of glazed pottery from two medieval sites in Benevento identified a group likely made locally. Some dark fragments may have been overfired rejects. The thirteenth- to fifteenth-century pottery tradition therefore preserves mistakes as well as attractive dishes. A pot that went wrong in the kiln can tell researchers how its successful neighbors were made.

The cathedral expanded during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, removing an older burial area in front of the church. Excavations beneath today’s floor distinguish those medieval changes from earlier churches and from modern rebuilding. A familiar place could be repeatedly reorganized as the community’s needs and ambitions changed.

Funerary inscriptions for ninth-century Lombard princes were reused in the cathedral’s later facade. Their words outlived the tomb arrangement for which they had been carved. The stones are now museum evidence of both the earlier dynasty and the practical medieval habit of reusing valuable building material.

A 2024 study brought scattered cathedral sculpture fragments back into conversation with one another. Its author proposed an earlier twelfth-century date for parts of the rebuilding and bronze door than some previous accounts had used. Reassembling fragments can change a building’s history; dates printed in older guides are not automatically the last word.

Santa Sofia’s twelfth-century cloister includes carvings of seasonal agricultural work, with months from June to December surviving. Other capitals display fantastic creatures. The sculptors placed familiar labor beside imaginative beasts, giving a person walking around the courtyard much more to look at than a row of plain supports.

An inscription in Santa Sofia’s cloister honors Abbot John IV, who governed from 1142 to 1176. Its Latin words “stat Quarti fama Iohannis” mean “the fame of John the Fourth endures.” This modern transcription comes from a carved capital and belongs to papal-era Benevento, after the Lombard dynasty had ended.

Beneventan was also the name of a distinctive handwriting style used across southern Italy. A regional example is the Montecassino Exultet roll of about 1075 to 1080, now British Library Add. 30337. It contains Latin for an Easter ceremony, with red musical signs above the words. Script, language and tune did different jobs on the same parchment.

On an Exultet roll, pictures faced the opposite direction from the words. As the reader let the scroll descend from the reading platform, listeners could see the images the right way up. This southern Italian format considered two audiences at once: the person singing the text and the people watching below.

The battle near Benevento on 26 February 1266 ended with Charles of Anjou defeating Manfred, king of Sicily. It belongs to the city’s later medieval setting, nearly two centuries after the Lombard dynasty ended. The battle’s famous name should not be mistaken for the fall of an independent Lombard duchy in 1266.

ending.text: Landulf VI’s death in 1077 ended the Lombard dynasty. Benevento continued as a papal city, with later occupations and local institutions. The imported 1279 endpoint is not the principality’s historical fall date.
